summary: BBN's announcement of a new proposed File Transfer Protocol document and a meeting at BBN on March 16 to try for final agreement. The proposal is an extensive update to RFC 354 intended to address objections raised against it. It is a proposal and meeting call, not a final standard.

eli5.summary: Someone rewrote the rules for sending files and invited everyone interested to a meeting to agree on them.

subtitle: A meeting call and a rewritten FTP proposal meant to settle the objections raised against RFC 354.

tldr.problem: RFC 354 drew objections, and the author wanted another attempt at final agreement on FTP.
tldr.mechanism: The memo attaches a proposed document that extensively updates RFC 354 and calls a meeting at BBN on March 16 to discuss it.
tldr.outcome: It is a proposal and meeting announcement, not a final standard. The unit metadata lists it as updating RFC 354.

today: The metadata gives this RFC's status as unknown and says it updates RFC 354. It lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Meeting Announcement
sections.content:
Alex McKenzie of BBN says the attached document is an extensive update to RFC 354 and, he believes, solves most of the objections to it. He calls a meeting of interested parties at BBN on March 16 to discuss it and other proposals.

The note is aimed at the whole network community, not just the old FTP committee. Attendees should know RFC 354 and also RFC 385, RFC 414, RFC 418 and RFC 438.
sections.eli5: The note says: here is a better draft, please come to a meeting and let us agree.

sections.title: Where the Proposal Came From
sections.content: The proposed document is the outcome of a meeting held 25 January 1973 in Cambridge, Massachusetts, with seven named participants from MIT and BBN. It is based on RFC 354, with considerations drawn from RFCs 385, 414, 418 and 438 and personal communication with network participants.
sections.eli5: A small group met, took the old rules and fixed them using everyone's comments.

sections.title: How It Differs from RFC 354
sections.content:
The model is the same: TELNET connections carry commands and replies, and a separate data connection carries files. The server listens on socket 3 for the user's ICP, and the user listens on the data socket before sending a transfer request.

Some points differ from RFC 354. Servers are required, not merely recommended, to implement the 8-bit byte size. EBCDIC is its own representation type. In ASCII representation any byte size other than 8 bits cancels the transfer request. The text says an EOF does not imply an EOR. A section on declarative specifications lists the minimum server implementation (ASCII type, Stream mode, File structure and commands such as USER, BYE, SOCK, RETR and STOR) and the initial defaults.
sections.eli5: Most of the plan is the same, but several maybes in the old draft became musts, and the minimum a server has to do is spelled out.

sections.title: A Typical Session
sections.content: The RFC ends with scenarios. In the first, a TIP user opens TELNET connections by ICP to host X on socket 3, logs in with USER and PASS, names a data socket with SOCK 65538, and requests a file with RETR. Host X replies with its own data socket, starts the transfer, and the user ends with BYE. A second scenario shows a user-FTP program prompting a person and failing a STOR with reply 451 Access denied.
sections.eli5: It shows a worked example: log in, say where to send the file, ask for it, say goodbye.
